html:
SMTO-DB-0008 — The database query names a table or column SMTO can't find

GUID: c5cf209f-294b-41f8-87e1-d3e1d2d59355
Slug: sql-schema-reference-invalid
Domain: DB · Subsystem: db

What happened

  • The query asks for a table or column that isn't in SMTO's list of what this database contains. The name may be wrong, or the database may have changed since SMTO last looked. No query was run.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If the Task is still running, wait. SMTO usually checks its list of tables and fixes the name itself. The error tells SMTO which table or column name didn't match.
  2. If tables or columns were added or renamed recently, ask SMTO in the conversation to look up this database's tables again before answering. SMTO keeps a saved list of the database's tables, and it may be older than your latest changes.
  3. If you know the exact table or column name, tell SMTO, for example "the column is called order_date". An exact name stops SMTO from guessing a similar but wrong one.
  4. Check that SMTO is using the right database: type @ in the conversation and pick the database entry you mean. The table may exist only in a different database than the one SMTO picked.

What success looks like

  • SMTO runs the query and shows results from the table you meant.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO, with the table or column name you expected. Don't let SMTO swap in a different table just because the name looks close.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • SQL classification rejected the query because it references a table or column absent from the cached schema of the selected database profile, including a column missing from its qualified table.

What this means

  • SQL classification compares referenced names against discovered schema sets and rejects unknown tables or columns, including a column missing from its qualified table. Input rejection is pre-dispatch only where the producer says so. Discovery and psql failures require their original execution evidence; diagnostics do not run SQL or prove that a mutation rolled back.

Why this can happen

  • SQL classification compares referenced names against discovered schema sets and rejects unknown tables or columns, including a column missing from its qualified table.

How to diagnose it

  • Check exact qualifiers and the snapshot's database/revision; stale discovery and mistaken names require different corrections.

How to fix it

  • Compare the names reported in Technical details with the selected profile's discovered schema. If the database changed, rerun database.discover_schema with refresh_schema=true for the exact parameter_key, then correct the table and column references from the refreshed schema. Do not guess replacement names, and do not reuse an old profile key or revision after the profile was edited.
  • Refresh schema discovery for the exact database and correct table/column references. Do not guess replacement names.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The corrected query references the intended current schema and passes classification.

What not to do

  • Do not submit a stale identifier or revision after another actor changed the resource.

Technical notes

  • Input rejection is pre-dispatch only where the producer says so. Discovery and psql failures require their original execution evidence; diagnostics do not run SQL or prove that a mutation rolled back.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
